question: The rapper Skrilla said of the drill song behind this meme that he never put an actual meaning on it and would not want to. The song was first released in December 2024 and officially released on 7 February 2025, and the meme spread through basketball edits featuring LaMelo Ball. The Overtime Elite player Taylen Kinney amplified it and launched a line of branded canned water. In a YouTube video by Cam Wilder posted on 31 March 2025, Maverick Trevillian became known as the kid behind it after yelling it while making an upward hand gesture. For 10 points, give this two-digit number, chosen by Dictionary.com as its 2025 Word of the Year despite having no real meaning.
answer: 67 [or six seven or 6-7 or six-seven or 6 7 or sixty-seven or sixty seven]

question: Its creator, an Indonesian TikTok user known as Noxa, made it on 28 February 2025 by asking DALL-E for a wake-up drum with a face and legs. It is an anthropomorphic kentongan, a traditional slit drum, and it carries either a wooden drumstick or a baseball bat. It became popular within Italian brainrot, a style of absurdist AI-generated content favoured by younger generations. It appeared in the Roblox game Steal a Brainrot, and its creator's legal team claimed copyright in it despite its AI origin. For 10 points, name this character, whose name pairs an onomatopoeia for its drum with the Indonesian term for the pre-dawn meal eaten during Ramadan.
answer: tung tung tung sahur [or tung tung sahur or tung sahur; prompt on "sahur"]

question: Its first episode, uploaded on 7 February 2023, ran for only 11 seconds. It is made in Source Filmmaker, using assets from Half-Life 2 and Counter-Strike: Source, by Alexey Gerasimov, who is known as Blugray and whose channel was formerly called DaFuq!?Boom! Its plot is a war between singing human-headed fixtures and an alliance of Cameramen, Speakermen and TV Men. Its videos had over 65 billion YouTube views by November 2023, and in July 2024 Michael Bay and Adam Goodman announced film and television adaptations. For 10 points, name this Generation Alpha animated series, whose title pairs a nonsense word with a bathroom fixture.

Early recorded uses include the 2003 Defari track For The Love, Gucci Mane's 2014 track On The Way and J. Cole's 2018 song Brackets. It comes from African American Vernacular English, where it originally conveyed respect for someone slightly older and more experienced. Its current meme sense took off in June 2021, when the TikTok user @callmechosen85 posted a video of a younger person greeting him with it, captioned as if he had officially reached a status. It is now used, often teasingly, for a man who seems older than his age, for example one who struggles with modern slang or grunts when sitting down. For 10 points, give this three-letter clipped form of a word for a parent's brother.

In the 2010s this term was used on forums such as Lookism.net, one of the so-called PSL forums, and it spread to TikTok in the early 2020s. It is associated with looksmaxxing, whose practices include mewing, a tongue-positioning technique, and pursuing hunter eyes and a defined jawline. The Kick livestreamer Clavicular, whose real name is Braden Peters, has been linked to promoting extreme forms of that practice. The framework built around it is widely criticised for promoting harassment. For 10 points, give this verb, a clipped form of an acronym for alpha male of the group, meaning to outshine someone in looks.
answer: mog [or mogging or mogged or mogs or to mog; prompt on "AMOG"]

question: According to the linguist John McWhorter, this word evolved from a common curse, and it has roots in Black Southern, Jamaican and wider African diaspora communities. The streamer YourRAGE said in a video that he always said it instead of the full curse, and that his chat began typing it in 2020 to mock him. The Twitch streamer Kai Cenat helped popularise it, and a TikTok video of 2 October 2023 featuring Fortnite characters was described by The New York Times as a key moment in its spread. The American Dialect Society nominated it for its 2023 Word of the Year. For 10 points, give this Twitch-born exclamation, a respelling of goddamn, that became a Generation Alpha meme.
answer: gyatt [or gyat or gyaat or gyattt; prompt on "gyat damn" or "gyatt damn"]

question: Its foundational idea, the Tropic Premise, was developed in the late 1950s by the British orthodontist John Mew, who argued that crooked teeth come mainly from poor tongue posture rather than genetics. Mew's son Mike brought the technique to YouTube in the 2010s, where an online following coined its name in his honor. It calls for pressing the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth to supposedly reshape the jaw and sharpen the profile over time, a claim no professional orthodontic body endorses. In November 2024, after a seven-year investigation that included a six-year-old patient who suffered seizure-like episodes, Mike Mew was struck off the UK's General Dental Council register. The practice is a staple of looksmaxxing communities alongside pursuing a defined jawline and so-called hunter eyes. For 10 points, name this pseudo-orthodontic tongue-posture technique named for its father-and-son promoters.

The double-x spelling in this term's suffix, later applied to everything from bulkmaxxing to sleepmaxxing, actually originated with this practice in 2010s incel forums, unlike the older single-x min-maxing from tabletop game theory. Its most dangerous fringe technique, bonesmashing, has people strike their own jaw and cheekbones with blunt objects on the mistaken belief that the trauma will make facial bones grow back sharper. Other adherents pursue surgical routes such as jaw contouring and leg-lengthening, or gentler steps like skincare and grooming. The Child Mind Institute has published guidance for parents after the trend spread from fringe forums to mainstream Gen Z apps such as TikTok in the early 2020s. It sits under a wider set of manosphere self-improvement practices that also include mewing and chasing a defined jawline. For 10 points, name this online obsession with maximizing one's physical attractiveness.

This entertainer's birth name is Felix Arvid Ulf Kjellberg, and he registered his channel in 2010 to post Let's Play videos of horror and action games. In 2017 he lost a partnership with Disney's Maker Studios after an antisemitic joke in one of his videos drew widespread criticism. His channel became YouTube's most-subscribed in August 2013 and held that title until being overtaken in April 2019 by the Indian label T-Series, a rivalry marked by his diss track Bitch Lasagna. He calls his fanbase the Bro Army and popularized the catchphrase Smash that like button. For 10 points, name this Swedish YouTuber, for years the platform's most-subscribed creator before being passed by T-Series and later by MrBeast.
answer: PewDiePie [or Felix Kjellberg or Felix Arvid Ulf Kjellberg; prompt on "Felix"]

question: Quality Control Music artists including Migos, Skippa Da Flippa, Rich The Kid and Peewee Longway are credited with creating this dance in Atlanta's hip-hop scene around 2013, and Migos say they debuted it while performing their song Emmitt Smith that November. It spread nationally in 2015 through a Migos single named after it and through Carolina Panthers quarterback Cam Newton's touchdown celebrations, one of which he later declared officially over. It is performed by dropping the head, raising one arm, and tucking the face into the crook of the other, bent arm, resembling a muffled sneeze. For 10 points, name this dance craze whose name is also used for a small hit of concentrated cannabis.

On 1 February 2002, the website WhatReallyHappened published one of the first pieces to summarize this claim, titled "The 9/11 Hijackings – An Inside Job?" Radio host Alex Jones began preaching it within weeks of the September 11 attacks, a stance that cost him more than seventy of his hundred-plus radio station affiliates. The low-budget 2005 documentary Loose Change pushed the claim to a much wider online audience, and the following year saw the founding of the group Architects & Engineers for 9/11 Truth. Its core assertion is that the U.S. government itself orchestrated the September 11 attacks as a false-flag operation, a claim overwhelmingly rejected by the engineering and intelligence communities. It has since become internet shorthand for any far-fetched conspiracy claim, often paired sarcastically with its sister catchphrase about jet fuel and steel beams. For 10 points, give this six-word slogan of the 9/11 Truth movement.
answer: 9/11 was an inside job [or 911 was an inside job]

question: The 2005 documentary Loose Change first popularized this claim as an argument that the World Trade Center towers must have come down by controlled demolition rather than the impact and fires from the planes that struck them. On 8 November 2014, the Redditor Sir-SmokesALot turned it into an absurdist non sequitur by editing it into a "Things a Pony Would Say" webcomic, having a cartoon horse blurt it out at random. The joke format spread through communities such as r/BlackPeopleTwitter and edited Winnie the Pooh comics in early 2015, and it is often abbreviated to a five-letter initialism. It is now used as a stock ironic non sequitur to derail a conversation with an unrelated claim from 9/11 conspiracy theories. For 10 points, give this nine-word truther catchphrase about a type of aircraft fuel and structural steel.

This app launched internationally in September 2017; in its original Chinese market it operates as a separate app called Douyin. Its parent company, ByteDance, merged it in August 2018 with Musical.ly, a lip-sync app it had bought for nearly a billion dollars the previous November, folding that app's mostly American teenage userbase into it. India banned it in 2020 alongside dozens of other Chinese apps amid a border clash with China. In April 2024, the U.S. president signed a law forcing its Chinese owner to divest it or face a ban in the country, and it became the first app to reach ten billion dollars in in-app spending. For 10 points, name this short-form video app known for its algorithmic For You feed.

Its original cooperative zombie-survival mode entered early access on 25 July 2017, developed by Epic Games. Inspired by the runaway success of PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds earlier that year, the studio built a hundred-player last-player-standing mode for it in about two months and released it free-to-play on 26 September 2017. That mode reached ten million players within its first two weeks and 125 million by June 2018. Players swing a pickaxe to harvest materials and build structures for cover, a mechanic that set it apart from its battle royale rivals. For 10 points, name this Epic Games title whose Battle Royale mode became a global pop-culture phenomenon.

In this video game's lore, the tech company Vindertech, founded by the character Vinderman, is credited with minting this currency, whose name is short for VinderTech Bucks. It buys only cosmetic items such as outfits, pickaxes, emotes and wraps that grant no competitive advantage, alongside battle passes. Under the game's original pricing scheme, buying 1,000 of them for real money has cost around ten US dollars, though a 2019 subscription service began granting players a monthly allotment on top of purchases. For 10 points, give this two-word, V-prefixed premium currency of the game Fortnite.

Sixteen-year-old Russell Horning, known as the Backpack Kid, performed this dance move on Saturday Night Live alongside Katy Perry in May 2017, catapulting it to viral fame. It involves swinging both arms front-to-back in unison on one side of the body while the hips swivel the opposite way. Epic Games added it as a purchasable emote in Fortnite's Season 2 Battle Pass that December, prompting Horning to sue the company in 2018 for using the move without his permission or compensation. That suit, along with four others filed against Epic over dance emotes, was withdrawn in 2019 after a Supreme Court copyright ruling required registering a work before suing over it. For 10 points, name this dance craze, also called the floss.

This entertainer was born Darren Jason Watkins Jr. on 21 January 2005 in Cincinnati, Ohio, and created his YouTube channel in 2016 to post gaming content. His livestreams of games like NBA 2K in December 2017 drew as few as two viewers at a time, but in 2021 clips of his energetic, often screaming reactions went viral on TikTok, earning him a million new subscribers within days. He soon became known for supporting the footballer Cristiano Ronaldo and, in 2022, signed to Warner Records to release the single "World Cup." He has since built a following for chaotic in-real-life streams filmed around the world. For 10 points, name this American YouTuber and streamer known by an energetic pseudonym.
answer: IShowSpeed [or Speed or Darren Watkins or Darren Jason Watkins Jr.; prompt on "Darren"]

question: This term first appeared on Urban Dictionary in 2012, the same year some accounts credit the Chicago rapper Chief Keef with popularizing it after using it on a music-video set. It began as an acronym, its three letters standing for a dismissive three-word phrase pointing out a woman across the room. Its use peaked around 2014 before making a slower comeback on platforms like Twitter and Reddit. Lexicographers now describe it as a widely sexist and disparaging slang word, generally aimed at a woman regarded as sexually promiscuous, even as some have tried to reclaim it. For 10 points, give this four-letter slang term, an acronym now used mostly as a slur against women.

Bronx-raised Twitch streamer Kai Cenat says this term started with him and his friend group, and he popularized it further with a 2022 video on how to get it. Actor Tom Holland helped push it into the mainstream during a June 2023 BuzzFeed interview. Many assume it derives from the middle syllable of a word for magnetic personal charm, though Cenat insists it isn't short for anything. Oxford named it its 2023 Word of the Year after more than 32,000 people, including language experts, weighed in. For 10 points, give this slang term for one's skill at charming or flirting with someone, often used in the phrase "rizz up."

The heavily edited black-and-white photos behind this meme come from a 2011 art project called Sleek'N'Tears by photographer Krista Sudmalis, starring the Russian fitness model Ernest Khalimov. A link to that photo series reached Reddit's bodybuilding forum on 15 October 2017, and the very next day it was reposted to 4chan, where users coined its name. That name combines a metric prefix meaning a billion with existing slang for a supremely confident, attractive man. It typically appears as a stoic, chiseled black-and-white portrait, often contrasted against a scrawny "virgin" counterpart in image macros. For 10 points, give this meme name for an exaggerated, larger-than-life ideal of masculinity.

Lexicographers dispute this term's exact origin: one theory traces it to an earlier British slang word for the willing partner of a dominant older man, dating to the 1920s or 30s, while another connects it to an American snack cake, in a sense recorded since 1963. Oxford Dictionaries instead places its coinage in the 1950s. It describes a slim, youthful-looking gay man with little or no body hair, and is often paired in queer slang with an opposite archetype, the bear. By the 1990s it was firmly part of mainstream queer vocabulary, though some critics call its disputed roots ageist. For 10 points, give this gay slang term for a young, slender man.

The 1998 comedy film Pecker helped popularize this term for an act performed by a stripper on a customer, well before gamers adopted it. Rapid crouching over an enemy's corpse in Quake or Counter-Strike as early as 1999 is sometimes cited as its first appearance in games, but the taunt truly took off with a 2001 shooter whose dead players could keep watching the action for a few seconds after being killed. Performing it means gloating over a defeated opponent by repeatedly crouching on top of their fallen body. It has sparked periodic controversy, with some critics likening the taunt to real-world sexual harassment. For 10 points, name this crouching-over-a-corpse taunt, named after a small bag of tea leaves.

This term grew out of "newbie," military slang used by American troops in the Vietnam War for a green recruit fresh to a unit. That older word jumped into early internet culture through the Usenet newsgroup talk.bizarre, with the earliest archived post using it dated 31 May 1988. As l33t-speak spread through 1990s programmer and gamer chatrooms, this shortened, deliberately misspelled offshoot broke off, often written with a zero in place of one of its vowels. Unlike a mere newbie, whose cluelessness is excused by inexperience, this one carries a harsher implication of persistent, incorrigible incompetence. The Concise Oxford English Dictionary added it in 2011. For 10 points, give this gaming slang term for an inexperienced or inept player.

The unrelated root of this term comes from an Old French word for the cuckoo bird, chosen because that species lays its eggs in another bird's nest. Partridge's Dictionary of Slang traces a shortened form of the word to fetish pornography, where by 2000 it had become a genre tag online. A harsher sense meaning "weakling" or "race traitor" emerged on 4chan in 2014 and quickly spread to Reddit. In August 2015 a hashtag combining it with a word for a mainstream conservative peaked during the Republican primary debates, and white nationalists have since used both the hashtag and its shortened form to attack Republican politicians deemed insufficiently hardline. For 10 points, give this pejorative slang term, shortened from a word for a man whose wife is unfaithful.

Far-right writer Theodore Robert Beale, who blogs under the pen name Vox Day, coined this term for a masculinity archetype on a nationalist blog in 2010, describing an introverted, aloof "lone wolf" as an alternative to a more extroverted dominant-male type. It borrows the eighteenth letter of the Greek alphabet as a label within a pseudoscientific hierarchy of male archetypes. On 25 January 2021, a tweet mocking a set of infographics using the term went viral, drawing over 25,000 retweets as most replies mocked the framework. It is now used mostly ironically online, often for a man who thinks he's being edgy and tough while looking anything but. For 10 points, give this Greek letter used as slang for a supposedly self-sufficient loner archetype of masculinity.

On TikTok in March 2024, the user lawfreeza posted a clip captioned "is this rizz" of two Instagram voice messages, the second of which uttered this phrase in response to being called corny. It riffs on Stewie Griffin's Family Guy catchphrase "Erm, what the deuce," swapping in a word already popularized by an unrelated masculinity-archetype meme. Viewers likened the voice's cadence to Squidward from SpongeBob SquarePants, and on 1 April 2024 the TikToker huugh_mungus dubbed the audio over a SpongeBob and Squidward clip, racking up over a million views within two days as a multi-screen "overstimulation" edit. It now functions as a catch-all expression of absurd, exaggerated confusion within so-called brainrot internet humor. For 10 points, give this three-word catchphrase of comic bewilderment that borrows the Greek letter also used for a lone-wolf masculinity archetype.
answer: what the sigma [or erm what the sigma; prompt on sigma]

question: This clipped form of a longer adjective functioned as English police jargon by the 1930s, tracing back further to Britain's 1824 "sus law," a stop-and-search statute that let officers arrest people on mere suspicion and whose discriminatory enforcement helped spark the 1981 Brixton riot. Black internet communities used the short form on forums years before Urban Dictionary's first entry for it appeared in August 2003, and Tyler, the Creator devoted a sketch to it on his show Loiter Squad in 2012. Its use exploded in August 2020 alongside a certain social deduction game's second wave of popularity, becoming the go-to word to call out a fellow crewmate. For 10 points, give this three-letter clipping of "suspicious," popularized among players of Among Us.

Oxford named this term its 2024 Word of the Year after its usage frequency rose 230 percent in a single year, following a public vote of more than 37,000 people. Oxford traces its first recorded use to Henry David Thoreau's 1854 book Walden, though its current sense describes a perceived decline in mental sharpness from consuming excessive trivial online content. It is closely associated with a broader vocabulary of nonsense internet slang popular with Generation Z and Generation Alpha, including terms like "Skibidi" and "Ohio." A subgenre of surreal AI-generated animal characters produced largely in Italy is often labeled with this term as a modifier. For 10 points, give this two-word term for supposed mental decline caused by too much low-quality online content.

The character behind this meme first appeared in a February 2017 YouTube review of Sonic Lost World by Gregzilla, who intentionally warped Knuckles the Echidna's design into a grotesque, googly-eyed figure. Fans of the Twitch streamer Forsen gave the character its national identifier, and its catchphrases, including asking "do you know de way," were lifted from the 2010 Ugandan action film Who Killed Captain Alex? A downloadable model of the character reached VRChat in September 2017, and a January 2018 video by YouTuber Jameskii turned it into a full-blown viral craze there. Its creator later expressed regret over the meme, which critics have condemned as a mockery of African accents. For 10 points, name this VRChat meme, a warped version of a Sonic the Hedgehog character given a fictional Ugandan identity.

This character debuted on Instagram on 15 June 2018, styled by his creators as a stylish traveler posing at real-world tourist spots such as Scotland's Doune Castle and the Isle of Skye. He is a CGI figure combining a realistic human male body with a detailed pig's head and snout, occupying the uncanny valley. On 21 March 2023, the TikTok user rover.joe overlaid one of his selfies with a fake incoming call screen and ringtone, and the resulting videos, captioned with a question asking whether you'll pick up, went viral within days. Users have since made horror, comedic and other remixes of the format. For 10 points, name this anthropomorphic pig-headed internet character, whose calls warrant an urgent decision.

Born in New York City in December 2001 to a Haitian father and Trinidadian mother, this streamer dropped out of SUNY Morrisville in 2020 to focus on content creation. He was recruited into the YouTube collective AMP by fellow Bronx creator Fanum after posting his first video in January 2018. He moved to Twitch in February 2021, and a month-long subathon in February 2023 made him the platform's most-subscribed streamer, a title he lost briefly to Ironmouse in September 2024 before reclaiming it the next month during his Mafiathon event. He is credited with popularizing internet slang terms including Rizz and Fanum tax. For 10 points, name this Twitch streamer known for chaotic collaborative content with his AMP collective.

This former kickboxer rose to notoriety as a social media personality after a brief 2016 stint on the British reality show Big Brother ended when a video surfaced of him hitting a woman, which producers said was consensual and which he denied any wrongdoing over. He was banned from Twitter in 2017 after writing that women bore some responsibility for being sexually assaulted, and he later built an online course called Hustler's University. On 29 December 2022, he was detained in Romania along with his brother Tristan on charges including human trafficking and rape, which he denies, and he was later ordered extradited to the United Kingdom to face separate charges there. For 10 points, name this British-American internet personality known for espousing hypermasculine and misogynistic views.
answer: Andrew Tate [or Emory Andrew Tate III; prompt on "Tate"]

question: This African American Vernacular English term is thought to derive from the phrase "crash dummy" and is often traced to rappers from Baton Rouge, Louisiana, including NBA YoungBoy. On December 18, 2023, the TikTok user @peezyante posted a video defining it that racked up over 1.7 million plays within three months. Used as a verb, it describes someone losing control and, often out of a feeling that they have nothing left to lose, deliberately jeopardizing their own body, relationships or future in a reckless outburst. People who do this habitually are given a noun form of the same two words, and the behavior is often compared online to a "meltdown". The term spread across TikTok in early 2024 and now appears constantly in captions about unhinged, self-destructive behavior after a breakup or provocation. For 10 points, give this two-word slang phrase for a reckless emotional or violent outburst, as in "he is about to ___".

This slang term combines "aura," internet shorthand for a person's charisma or presence, with a gaming term for repeatedly grinding to accumulate a resource. TikTok user h.chua_212 posted an early example of the phrase in January 2024, captioning a video of friends bowling. It exploded into a worldwide phenomenon in mid-2024 after a clip spread of an eleven-year-old Indonesian boy, Rayyan Arkan Dikha, calmly swaying atop the bow of a traditional racing boat during Riau's Pacu Jalur festival while his teammates paddled below him. His unbothered poise was hailed online as the ultimate example of the practice, and imitators worldwide have restaged his pose ever since. A related 2026 trend called "aura battles" saw participants competing head-to-head through posing, mogging and dancing to see who could accumulate the most of this quality. For 10 points, name this slang term for accumulating charisma points through a deliberately cool-looking repeated action, popularized by a dancing Indonesian boat boy.

According to Merriam-Webster, this word has carried the sense of "done for" or "finished" since the nineteenth century, but its current internet usage traces to Australian slang, where it meant ruined, broken or ridiculous before spreading through gaming and hip-hop circles to also mean wasted, dazed or defeated. It doubles as a synonym for "roasted," describing someone who has just been savagely mocked or insulted. Streamers and gamers now use it to describe an unwinnable, hopeless position, often invoking the rhetorical question "chat, am I ___?" to ask an audience whether a situation is truly beyond saving. It can also simply describe exhaustion after a long day or embarrassment after a mistake. For 10 points, give this past-participle slang adjective, food-preparation vocabulary reused online for being finished, doomed or humiliated.

This phrase traces to African American Vernacular English, where the verb "to cap" has meant "to lie," "boast," or "exaggerate" since at least the early twentieth century, feeding into the ritualized insult exchanges known as "capping" that flourished in Black communities by the 1960s. Geto Boys rapper Willie D used a related form, "high cappin'," on a 1989 track, and Atlanta hip-hop artists such as Young Thug and Future later popularized this exact two-word phrase in their own lyrics. Now ubiquitous on TikTok and Twitter, it functions as an assurance that the speaker is being completely honest, while its bare, one-word negation instead accuses someone of lying or exaggerating. For 10 points, give this two-word Gen Z catchphrase, an assurance of sincerity built by negating a slang word for "lie".

Used adverbially since the 1800s to describe something restrained or subdued, this word's modern slang sense of "secretly," "quietly," or "to some extent" is widely credited to African American Vernacular English. It softens whatever statement follows it, letting a speaker admit something mildly embarrassing or understated without fully committing to it, as when confessing to secretly enjoying something uncool. It rose to ubiquity on Twitter, Instagram and Snapchat during the 2010s before becoming one of the most common slang words in English-language memes and captions, often paired with an antonym describing something done openly and intensely. For 10 points, give this hyphenated slang adverb meaning "somewhat" or "secretly," whose opposite is "highkey".

At Axum, this word was used as a royal title as early as the reign of King Ezana around 250 AD, and in pre-1974 Ethiopia it named a rank bestowed on a regional ruler by the Negusa Nagast, or "King of Kings," the title by which Ethiopia's emperors were formally known. On June 2, 2007, twelve-year-old Andrew Lay was asked to spell this word at the Scripps National Spelling Bee; after he requested its language of origin and a definition, a judge explained that "the ___ ruled Ethiopia until the coup of 1974," and the boy's visibly nervous reaction to a word that sounds almost exactly like a well-known racial slur made the clip a long-running internet meme. Some writers have controversially proposed a direct link between this word and that slur, though most linguists instead trace the slur to Latin and Iberian words for "black". For 10 points, give this Ethiopian Semitic title for "king" that a nervous spelling bee contestant once had to define on camera.

In 2013 this animated film's screenplay began circulating across Tumblr and Pastebin as a full-script copypasta, its opening line reading "According to all known laws of aviation, there is no way a bee should be able to fly." Comment sections and chat windows became flooded with its entire dialogue, forcing several platforms to adjust how they displayed walls of unbroken text. Around 2015 and 2016, YouTubers built a whole remix genre around it, including a video by creator AvoidAtAllCosts that plays the film but speeds it up every time a certain insect is mentioned on screen. Its plot follows a recent college graduate named Barry B. Benson, voiced by Jerry Seinfeld, who sues the human race for stealing honey. For 10 points, name this 2007 DreamWorks animated film whose screenplay became a legendary internet copypasta.

On January 14, 2013, an anonymous 4chan poster kicked off a cult internet obsession with this film by posting a rambling greentext story proclaiming its title character to be both "love" and "life." Devotees of that meme, who called themselves "brogres," kept the joke alive online through its peak in late 2014. Loosely based on a 1990 picture book by William Steig, it follows a solitary, onion-loving ogre voiced by Mike Myers who agrees to rescue a princess in order to reclaim his swamp from banished fairy-tale creatures. Its soundtrack's use of Smash Mouth's "All Star" has since become a meme of its own. For 10 points, name this 2001 DreamWorks animated film about a green ogre, subject of the "is love, is life" copypasta.

This rapper, born Daniel Hernandez, built an early online following through his rainbow-colored hair and heavily tattooed face, breaking out with his 2017 single "Gummo." His affiliation with the Nine Trey Gangsta Bloods led to his November 2018 arrest on racketeering and firearms charges, including conspiracy to commit murder. He avoided a lengthy sentence by taking the stand in 2019 and testifying against his own former associates, a move that made him a widely mocked online symbol of "snitching," complete with rat-themed edits and memes. Days after his release from home confinement in May 2020, he dropped the single "Gooba," whose music video briefly set a record for the most views in 24 hours on YouTube. For 10 points, name this rapper and internet punching bag, also known by a number-based nickname derived from his stage name.

This catchphrase was first voiced by British actor Zoe Lister for a television advert released by its airline on December 23, 2022, set to Jess Glynne's song "Hold My Hand." A new version of that ad, uploaded to the airline's YouTube channel in January 2024, showed a family enjoying a carefree package holiday. Starting in March 2025, TikTok users began dubbing Lister's cheerful voiceover over clips of holiday disasters instead, such as sunburns, airport meltdowns and cancelled flights, milking the ironic contrast between the chipper narration and the chaos on screen. The trend went on to soundtrack more than 1.3 million videos, and the airline itself leaned into the joke rather than fight it. For 10 points, give this six-word slogan for a British package-holiday airline, now a byword for vacations gone hilariously wrong.
answer: Nothing beats a Jet2 holiday [or Nothing beats a Jet2holiday; prompt on Jet2]

question: This character is often cited as the biggest breakout hit of a wider genre of surreal AI-generated animal-object hybrids known as Italian brainrot, a genre whose first viral entry, a Nike-wearing shark called Tralalero Tralala, appeared on TikTok in January 2025, followed a month later by a bomb-dropping crocodile hybrid called Bombardiro Crocodilo. Like those characters, it is narrated in an exaggerated, AI-generated Italian-accented voice reciting absurd, rhyming nonsense. Unlike most of its genre-mates, though, its name and design draw on Indonesian rather than Italian culture, referencing a traditional wooden slit drum used to wake a village for a pre-dawn Ramadan meal. For 10 points, name this anthropomorphic drum-on-legs meme character, whose thrice-repeated name imitates the sound of that drum.
answer: tung tung tung sahur [or tung tung sahur or tung sahur; prompt on "sahur"]

question: In November 2025, the companies behind a Roblox game sued the agency Mementum Lab in California's Northern District, seeking a declaratory judgment that the agency holds no U.S. copyright in this character on the grounds that AI-generated works fail copyright law's human-authorship requirement; Mementum countersued for trademark infringement, and a jury trial in that case is scheduled for November 2027. The Roblox game at the center of that suit, Do Big Studios' Steal a Brainrot, had earlier received a cease-and-desist letter over the character and briefly removed it before an unauthorized reintroduction sparked the litigation; that game would go on to peak at over 25 million concurrent players. Its Indonesian creator, an artist billed online only by an alias, has said the design took just fifteen minutes and seven prompts to generate, after an AI image tool badly misread a wooden slit drum called a kentongan as a stick-limbed creature wielding a bat. For 10 points, name this litigated meme character, an Indonesian entry in the Italian brainrot genre whose thrice-repeated name imitates the sound of a drum used to wake villagers for a pre-dawn Ramadan meal.
answer: tung tung tung sahur [or tung tung sahur or tung sahur; prompt on "sahur"]
